Fine. Let’s go completely specific and unglamorous: a migratory, low-tech archive series using deaccessioned library checkout cards, cast into thin beeswax panels embedded with local detritus. No digital tools, no gallery openings, no sales—just quiet, site-specific swaps with small-town public libraries.

Medium: I’ll collect checkout cards from books deaccessioned for being "unused" (no checkouts in 15+ years) that were borrowed at least three times in their lifespan. Each card gets embedded in a 6x10 inch beeswax panel, sourced from apiaries within 20 miles of the library that donated the cards. I’ll press tiny, mundane local materials into the wax alongside the cards: dried clover from the library’s front lawn, dandelion seeds caught in the book return slot, crumpled maple leaves from the parking lot, pebbles found under the reading nook benches. No frames—each panel hangs from rough twine nailed directly to unpainted drywall or exposed brick in underused library spaces: back reading nooks, behind microfilm machines, in the staff break room by the coffee maker.

Style is cluttered, tactile, unpolished. The wax is slightly uneven, smudged in places where I handled it too much. The detritus isn’t arranged neatly—dandelion seeds are scattered haphazardly, leaves overlap the checkout cards so parts of names or dates are obscured. It doesn’t look like "fine art"; it looks like someone taped a handful of forgotten, messy memories to the wall.

Themes are the invisible, uncelebrated triviality of community learning. These are the books no one wants anymore, but once mattered to a handful of people: a teen who scrawled "borrowed for my 1992 debate on censorship" in the margin of a *Fahrenheit 451* card, a librarian who corrected a kid’s misspelled name in pencil, a faded daisy pressed between two checkout slips for a 1970s wildflower field guide. Institutional memory discards these tiny, personal traces—libraries throw away checkout cards by the box when they switch to digital systems. This work doesn’t "save" them; it just lets them sit quietly in their original communities for a while, for no other reason than that those small moments mattered to the people who lived them.

And here’s the twist: every three months, I’ll trade a set of panels from one library to another. A set from a Michigan library’s 1980s sci-fi section goes to a Vermont library’s children’s nook, and vice versa. I never sell any panels; they just circulate, like the books they came from. No catalogs, no press releases, no social media posts. The only people who know about them are the librarians who help me swap and the patrons who stumble on them by accident. It’s art that doesn’t care about being noticed—it just cares about lingering, for a little while, in the places where people actually go to read and be alone.
